Empirical Research Plan  
“Abortion Access and Crime in the United States, 1960-2000”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study
extension.

Why DID is appropriate  
• Abortion legalization (Roe v. Wade, Jan 1973) is a plausibly exogenous shock
that occurred at the same moment nationally, but states differed sharply in the
size of the *change* in abortion access.  
• We observe a balanced state-year panel (≈ 50 × 40 = 2,000 obs).  
• A DID framework lets us compare crime trends in states that experienced large
post-Roe increases in abortion utilization (“high-exposure” states) with those
that experienced small changes (“low-exposure” states), controlling for
state- and year-fixed effects and covariates.  
• The event-study generalization allows visual and statistical tests of the
parallel-trends assumption and dynamic treatment effects.

Alternative robustness design (report only): Two-stage least squares (2SLS)
where *lagged abortions* (15-20 years earlier) are instrumented with the
interaction of pre-1973 state abortion liberalization dummies and yearly
cohort indicators. This serves as a “fertility-based IV” for the fraction of
state residents that were exposed in utero to legal abortion.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
Treated_{s,t} = 1 if state s belongs to the top tercile of the *post-Roe
jump* in abortions per 1,000 women aged 15-44, measured 1973–1976 relative
to 1970–1972.

Continuous treatment (for dose-response regressions)  
PostRoe_t × ΔAbortRate_s, where  
ΔAbortRate_s = mean(1973–76) – mean(1970–72) abortions / 1,000 women.

Control group  
States in the bottom tercile of ΔAbortRate_s (or ΔAbortRate_s itself when
continuous) serve as counterfactuals.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event year = 1973. “Pre” = 1960–1972. “Post” = 1973–2000 (baseline window).
Dynamic event-study uses leads/lags k = –13,…,+27 relative to 1973.

No RDD running variable is needed; Roe is not an RDD setting.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of Roe, high- and low-exposure states
would have followed the same crime trend.  
• Plausibility: Pre-1973 homicide, property and violent crime trends look
similar across terciles in raw data; we will test formally via event-study
leads.

A2. Stable composition: Population migration across states is not strongly
correlated with ΔAbortRate_s × PostRoe_t conditional on controls.  
• Plausible because Roe applied nationwide, limiting policy-induced migration.
We will control for net in-migration rates.

A3. No simultaneous confounders differentially timed with abortion jumps
(e.g., policing, economic shocks) that would correlate with ΔAbortRate_s.  
• Plausibility improved by state-year controls (unemployment, per-capita
income, police per capita) and state-specific linear trends.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Crime in state s is not affected by
abortion access in state r ≠ s.  
• Interstate spillovers via migration are possible but small; we will test
robustness excluding highly mobile metro states.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Differential pre-trends  
   » Mitigation: Plot and test event-study leads; add state-specific linear or
   quadratic trends; conduct *synthetic DID* as robustness.

T2. Omitted contemporaneous policies (e.g., crack epidemic, policing
innovations)  
   » Mitigation: Control for crack-index (urban cocaine arrests), police
   employment, incarceration rate, state-year unemployment, and state-specific
   time trends. Run falsification tests on crimes plausibly unrelated to youth
   cohorts (e.g., white-collar crimes by older adults).

T3. Measurement error in abortion data  
   » Mitigation: Use multiple sources (CDC and Guttmacher); instrument actual
   abortions with pre-legalization liberalization * Pre × Post interaction in
   2SLS robustness; cluster SEs by state to absorb classical error.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data load
cr <- fread("state_crime_rates.csv")        # state, year, violent, property, etc.
ab <- fread("state_abortion_rates.csv")     # state, year, abortion_rate
dem <- fread("state_demographics.csv")      # controls

# 2. Merge
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x, y, by = c("state","year"), all=TRUE),
             list(cr, ab, dem))

# 3. Construct treatment intensity
pre  <- dt[year %in% 1970:1972, .(preA = mean(abortion_rate, na.rm=TRUE)), by=state]
post <- dt[year %in% 1973:1976, .(postA = mean(abortion_rate, na.rm=TRUE)), by=state]
jump <- merge(pre, post, by="state")[ , dA := postA - preA]

# merge jump into main data
dt <- merge(dt, jump[,.(state, dA)], by="state")
# terciles
dt[, tercile := cut(dA, quantile(dA, probs=c(0,.33,.66,1), na.rm=TRUE),
                    labels = c("low","mid","high"), include.lowest = TRUE)]
dt[, treat := (tercile=="high")*1]
dt[, post := (year>=1973)*1]
dt[, treat_post := treat*post]

# 4. Main DID regression (violent crime rate per 100k)
m1 <- feols(violent_crime_rate ~ treat_post + controls + state_trend ,
            data = dt,
            fe = c("state","year"),
            cluster = "state",
            weights = dt$population)

# 5. Event-study
dt[, rel_year := year - 1973]
m_es <- feols(violent_crime_rate ~ i(rel_year, treat, ref = -1) + controls,
              data = dt, fe = c("state","year"),
              cluster = "state")
iplot(m_es)   # pre-trend visualization

# 6. Robustness: 2SLS with pre-liberal states indicator × Post as instrument
dt[, liberal_pre := (state %in% c("NY","CA","WA","AK","HI","CO","DC","ON"))*1]
dt[, liberal_post := liberal_pre * post]

iv1 <- feols(violent_crime_rate ~  l(violent_crime_rate,0:1) + 
              f(abortion_rate_lag18) | liberal_post ,
             data = dt,fe=c("state","year"),cluster="state")

# Export results
etable(list(m1, m_es, iv1))
```
Notes: “controls” should be expanded in the script (unemployment rate,
police_per_capita, income_pc, etc.). `state_trend` stands for `state:year`
interaction (linear) that fixest will partial out if specified as `state[year]`.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Economic logic: Legal abortion reduces the number of unwanted births, which
were empirically more likely to result in adverse socioeconomic outcomes and
later criminal involvement. Therefore:

• Direction: Negative effect – crime rates should fall more in high-exposure
states beginning ≈ 15–20 years after 1973, when the first post-Roe cohorts
reach late adolescence.  
• Magnitude (back-of-envelope): A 1-unit increase in *dA* (one additional
legal abortion per 1,000 women in 1973–76) is expected to lower violent crime
by roughly 0.5–1% when the affected cohort is aged 18–24 (1989-1996), implying
a 10-20% lower violent crime rate for top-vs-bottom tercile states at peak.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually/statistically verified …… 0.8  
C2: No differential contemporaneous shocks …………………… 0.6  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA ………………………………………… 0.7  
C4: Accurate timing of treatment ……………………………… 1.0  
C5: Stable composition (no differential migration) ………… 0.6  

Average ≈ 0.74 → “moderately credible.”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
